A growing number of Germans are not attracted by Berlin Image: Jens Kalaene/dpa Advertisement Skip next section What you need to know What you need to know More Germans think Berlin 'lacks charisma' than those who find it 'fascinating,' according to a survey Panda twins Leni and Lotti celebrate their second birthday at Berlin Zoo The German government is reportedly considering sanctioning a Russian cultural center in the capital over the recent drone incident at Leipzig airport Nearly a quarter of German companies are facing a shortage of skilled workers This is a roundup of the stories making headlines in Germany on Friday, August 21 2026: Skip next section At least 8 injured after car crashes into storefront in Hesse 08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 At least 8 injured after car crashes into storefront in Hesse The driver was taken to hospital in a critical condition Image: Fotoreport-DB/HessenNewsTV/dpa/picture alliance At least eight people sustained minor injuries after a car appeared to lose control and hit people in a pedestrian-only section in Hofgeismar in the central German state of Hesse . Police cited witnesses as saying that the driver of the car appeared to have been experiencing medical difficulties right before the incident unfolded. Locals noticed the man behind the wheel at a crosswalk and approached him to help, but he sped into the pedestrian zone and hit several people. His car ultimately came to a stop after he crashed into a storefront. Other passersby immediately offered help to the driver, who has now been taken to hospital, where his condition is reportedly critical, according to police. The accident site remains cordoned off. The incident took place around 10:30 a.m. local time Image: Fotoreport-DB/HessenNewsTV/dpa/picture alliance https://p.dw.com/p/5JCNF Skip next section Berlin weighing sanctions against Russian cultural center over Leipzig drone incident 08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 Berlin weighing sanctions against Russian cultural center over Leipzig drone incident Russia operates a large cultural center in the German capital Image: Jochen Eckel/IMAGO Amid mounting evidence that Russia was behind the planned drone attack on Leipzig Airport this month, the German government is reportedly considering imposing sanctions on the controversial Russian House cultural center in Berlin . German government officials have avoided publicly blaming Moscow for the incident, in which an explosive-laden drone was found at the airport in Leipzig. But according to Der Spiegel , Berlin is weighing possible sanctions against Russia, including targeting the Russian House on Friedrichstrasse. Moscow says it is a cultural center, but security officials in Germany suspect it is also used for espionage activities. Despite the frosty ties between Berlin and Moscow in recent years, Germany has resisted closing the center for fear that Russia would retaliate by closing Goethe Institutes in Moscow and St. Petersburg — the last remaining representations of German civil society in Russia. https://p.dw.com/p/5JC3N Skip next section Almost 1/4 of German companies face shortage of skilled workers 08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 Almost 1/4 of German companies face shortage of skilled workers Germany is facing a nationwide shortage of skilled labor Image: Tamir Kalifa/Getty Images Nearly one in four companies in Germany are facing a lack of skilled workers, the Munich-based ifo institute said Friday. The survey found that 23.2% of German firms had reported a shortage of skilled staff in July, a 2-point increase since April. The long-term average of German companies reporting skilled labor shortages remains much higher, at 31.7%. A "weak economy" is currently limiting demand for skilled workers, ifo researcher Daria Schaller said. But she warned that as Germany's economy recovers, "the shortage of skilled workers is likely to increase considerably again." Demand rose most sharply in the telecommunications sector, where 31.1% of firms were lacking skilled workers, compared to 16.3% in April. Nearly 65% of companies in the consultancy and auditing sectors were facing skilled labor shortages, up from 52.4%. "It is therefore a historic low." Find out why Germany's gas storage levels are so low in this in-depth report by DW's Nik Martin. https://p.dw.com/p/5JC1x Skip next section Panda twins celebrate second birthday at Berlin Zoo 08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 Panda twins celebrate second birthday at Berlin Zoo Leni (right) and Lotti (left) both have names with connections to Berlin Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance Berlin Zoo held a birthday party for two of its most popular residents: twin pandas Leni and Lotti, who are turning two years old this weekend. The panda cubs were treated to a special ice cake made of beetroot and carrot juice, which was waiting for them on the climbing frame in their outdoor enclosure, Berlin Zoo said in a statement. "The two panda twins devoured the icy birthday surprise with obvious enthusiasm," the zoo said. The twin sisters still regularly seek out mother Meng Meng to play with her, the zoo said Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance Born on August 22, 2024 , the sisters have grown from tiny cubs weighing less than 170 grams (under 6 ounces) each into giant pandas. Leni weighs more than 70 kilograms (154 pounds), while Lotti weighs around 61 kilograms. "Two years ago, Leni and Lotti could still fit in our hands; today, together they weigh more than 130 kilograms. Watching them develop is very special for our entire team. As true Berliners, they have long since found many fans in the city," said Zoo and Animal Park Director Dr. Andreas Knieriem. The pandas' names have a special connection to Berlin: Leni is named after iconic German actress and Berlin native Marlene Dietrich , while Lotti is named after Charlottenburg, which neighbors the zoo. Leni and Lotti are their mother's second litter since China gifted Meng Meng to Germany in 2017 Image: John Macdougall/AFP Their mother Meng Meng arrived in Germany in 2017 as part of an agreement with China, which has gifted pandas to friendly nations as part of its "panda diplomacy" policy . China maintains ownership of the animals and any cubs that are produced, and virtually all cubs born outside China are eventually returned. Knieriem said Leni and Lotti are "ambassadors for a species whose protection can only succeed through international cooperation. Because we mustn't forget that fewer than 2,000 giant pandas live in their natural habitat." The giant panda is listed as "vulnerable" to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). https://p.dw.com/p/5JC0w Skip next section Berlin not as appealing to Germans today compared to 20 years ago — survey 08/21/2026 August 21, 2026 Berlin not as appealing to Germans today compared to 20 years ago — survey Graffiti and grime are common sights on many of Berlin's streets Image: Joko/picture alliance A new survey has found that Berlin is losing its appeal to many Germans. An Allensbach Institute poll published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on Friday found that 31% of respondents consider their capital city to be a "fascinating metropolis." The same survey found that 36% of the 1,039 people polled think Berlin lacks charisma. The figures represent a sharp decline in Berlin's appeal among Germans. A previous Allensbach survey from 2007 showed that 66% thought the capital was "fascinating," with only 14% saying it lacked appeal. Famously described by former mayor Klaus Wowereit as "poor but sexy," Berlin has seen tens of thousands of workers move to the city, causing rents to soar. This has in turn placed increasing strain on world-famous Berlin's nightclubs , many of which are being priced out by property developers. Hamburg (48%) and Munich (47%) lead the way for Germans who were asked which cities are particularly appealing. Asked which cities they would not want to live in, Berlin scored 46%, making it the least popular city alongside financial capital Frankfurt am Main . https://p.dw.com/p/5JBpt Skip next section Welcome to our coverage Published 08/21/2026 Published August 21, 2026 last updated 08/21/2026 last updated August 21, 2026 Welcome to our coverage Karl Sexton | Zac Crellin Editor Guten Morgen! from Bonn, where the long-overdue rain from the past two days has eased ahead of the weekend. Log in here » RIGA – As Russian threats escalate in Latvia, a Canadian-led NATO mission is strengthening its presence near the Russian and Belarusian borders. The Canadian Press observed the increasing tensions on the ground. In the early hours of Aug. 14, residents in four areas of the region received a phone alert, including in Daugavpils, Latvia’s second-largest city. A Latvian soldier takes a photo of a drone launch during the Baltic trust exercise, organized by NATO in Selijas, Latvia, on Aug. 14, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Stéphane Blais The alert urged citizens to take shelter due to a “potential threat” detected in the airspace. Jana, a Russian-speaking Latvian woman whom The Canadian Press met outside a church in Daugavpils, was among the tens of thousands of people who received the alert. “Obviously, it’s very worrying to receive this kind of message. We worry about our family, about our loved ones. Only crazy people aren’t worried,” said Jana, who did not want to give her full name to the media. A few hours after the alert, authorities announced that a drone loaded with explosives originating from Belarus had violated Latvian airspace before being shot down by NATO fighter jets. No injuries were reported. Tensions between Latvia, Moscow and Minsk have increased to the point where Latvian Prime Minister Evika Silina was forced to resign last May, following repeated incursions by unmanned aerial vehicles into the country’s territory. The Canadian Press met with Canadian Col. David Brassard, the newly appointed commander of the NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia, at the Adazi military base, located in the centre of the country. He took office on June 10, two weeks after Silina’s resignation. Since then, he says three drones have been shot down. “The security situation we are currently experiencing in the east is what I call a ‘hybrid’ situation,” he said. “Hybrid” attacks refer to hostilities that do not necessarily constitute formal acts of war but aim to destabilize governments and sow confusion among the population. Those responsible for such acts are not always easily identifiable. “It’s not as if there were Russian flags attached to the drones; it can be difficult to assign blame,” said Brassard. Some of these drones are reportedly Ukrainian drones that were diverted into Latvian airspace by Russian jamming, he added. Maj.-Gen. Arnoud Stallmann of NATO’s Allied Command Transformation does not hesitate to use the word “war” to describe the situation. “We have truly come to terms with the threat from Russia; even though, at this stage, we call it hybrid war, I think we are actually at war,” Stallmann said during a NATO exercise in Selijas, central Latvia, in mid-August. The Canadian mission aims to “reassure, deter, and defend,” and is adapting to the escalation of hostile acts. Since the mission’s launch in 2017, Canadian troops — numbering between 1,500 and 1,600 — have been stationed in Adazi. But they will now be increasingly deployed, sometimes on a permanent basis, to various strategic locations near the borders with Russia and Belarus. “This is just the beginning. We’re in the process of expanding between now and Christmas,” said Brassard, noting that a first permanent platoon is now stationed in the Russian-speaking city of Daugavpils. “There are subversive activities taking place around Daugavpils, a culturally Russian region with strong ties to Russia,” Brassard said. In Latvia, Russian speakers account for about 30 per cent of the total population. In Daugavpils, the proportion is closer to 80 per cent. On the streets of Daugavpils, several residents interviewed by The Canadian Press are opposed to NATO’s military presence in their city. “We don’t need NATO. I see Canadian soldiers in the city, always eating kebabs. Why are they here? I don’t understand what purpose they serve,” said Mikhail, a 55-year-old man who served in the Soviet Army. Inna Plavoka, editor-in-chief of the independent media outlet Chayka, which publishes content primarily in Russian, is more sympathetic to NATO. “It may be hard for a Canadian to understand their position, but you have to realize that Russian propaganda is so effective at brainwashing people,” she said. When the war in Ukraine broke out, she says many believed “the Russians will take care of the Ukrainians and then come to save us.” When she asked who they wanted to be saved from, “they made the usual argument that the Russian language is being suppressed.” In Latvia, a country that endured 50 years of Soviet occupation, many Russian speakers feel discriminated against due to national policies that restrict the use of Russian in education and public spaces. Russian President Vladimir Putin often uses the pretext of defending Russian-speaking populations to justify his offensives in Ukraine. Latvian speakers generally hold a very positive view of the Canadian presence. A 2022 study by the University of Greifswald in Germany in collaboration with the Latvian research centre SKDS found that 79 per cent of them described Canadian soldiers as being professional or friendly. The same study shows that 34 per cent of Russian speakers find it difficult to characterize Canadian troops. Brassard says his troops are “prepared” for a Russian incursion into Latvia, adding he has “all the capabilities (he) needs” to deal with an attack. How likely is a Russian attack? “It’s a question of capabilities and intentions,” answers Janis Kazocins, who served as the Latvian president’s national security adviser from 2016 to 2023. He says the Kremlin would “certainly” intend to take economic, political and military control of the Baltic states if possible. “The real question is whether the Russians are willing to risk a nuclear war over a small town in northeastern Estonia or Latvia,” he argued. But Kazocins, who is now with the Riga Center for Geopolitical Studies, does not believe there’s a serious risk of a conventional attack against NATO. “Russia does not have the capacity to open a new front,” he says. “It simply wouldn’t work, especially since we have people — like your fellow Canadians — who actively support us on the ground and who, in the event of an attack, will fight.” Young people have also expressed their willingness to fight for their country. A drone believed to come from Belarus, was shot down on the eve of the 825 anniversary of Latvia’s capital of Riga. As the city celebrated, NATO organized a public event in front of a museum. Tanks were on display, and soldiers, flanked by NATO and Canadian flags, were talking with residents. Among them was Loreta Munda, a 17-year-old who plans to pursue a career in the military. “When I was younger, in 2014, I saw on the news what was happening in Ukraine. I thought to myself, ‘My God, if that happens here, I want to be among those who protect my country.’” With NATO forces present, Loreta says she feels safe. “I know there are soldiers ready to help us, but there are also plenty of people my age who are ready to defend our country.” In a country where the scars of Soviet history remain raw, Latvia is caught between Russian threats and the support of its NATO allies. — This report was produced with a grant from the Fonds québécois en journalisme international. This report was first published by The Canadian Press Aug. 22, 2026. Photograph: Chris Radburn/Reuters UK news Two Latvian men arrested at RAF base in Cambridgeshire used by US military Men aged 32 and 36 detained on suspicion of trespass, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Thu 8 Oct 2026 17.27 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 11.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Latvian men were arrested in the early hours of Thursday after they were discovered inside the perimeter of RAF Molesworth, a Cambridgeshire base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations. The men, 32 and 36, were picked up at 2am inside the base, in an investigation that began four hours earlier when military police discovered an abandoned vehicle outside the facility. Military police, helped by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence before finding and arresting the men, initially on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. The suspects, Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK. Counter-terror police are now leading the investigation due to the nature of the incident, which comes a few days after the US withdrew B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire amid concerns about a possible Iran-directed attack. Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counter-terrorism policing London, said there was nothing at this stage to suggest a connection to September’s incident near RAF Fairford, but said investigators were yet to determine what the men had been doing. “Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and inquiries are very much ongoing,” she added. Investigators said it was unclear at this stage if there was a hostile state link to the men’s presence on the base, if they were criminals or whether they had ended up on the site in a misjudged state of late-night exuberance. The abandoned vehicle was taken to a nearby police location. Initial searches led concerned officers to call in explosives specialists to carry out further checks, though nothing concerning was understood to have been found. A police cordon was also briefly imposed on part of the A1 south of Peterborough and around the village of Glatton, as a precaution, but has been lifted. Officers were carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation, counter-terror police added in a statement. Both men remained in police custody on Thursday. RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre, which provides military intelligence to Nato, and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe, which provides similar service for the US military’s European command, though not Centcom, which is responsible for Iran. View image in fullscreen The two Latvian nationals were arrested after breaching the perimeter fence of the military base. Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images The head of the armed forces, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, said he had “confidence around the safety and security of our bases” as he visited troops on a military exercise in Wales earlier on Thursday. The chief of defence staff cited the “enormously close relationships from an intelligence perspective and operationally with the US” as reasons for his confidence, but said the US had removed its bombers from Fairford as a precaution. “The decision to remove the bombers, which don’t ordinarily live there … to take them back was an operational decision to reduce the risk,” he added. The bombers were suddenly redeployed on Sunday, amid reports that the US feared Iran could orchestrate a drone attack on B-1 planes on the ground. British sources remain sceptical that Iran would have the capability to launch an attack of such sophistication, though the investigation into why five men driving three white vans descended on a village next to Fairford continues. Mark Rowley, the Met police chief, said the public would “see more progress on this investigation”, and urged them to trust the police as they worked with spy agencies MI5, GCHQ and intelligence partners internationally. The five men arrested near RAF Fairford, all British nationals in their 20s from London, have been released on police bail without charge, as has a sixth, a dual UK-Iranian national, who was arrested subsequently. A seventh man, aged 22, who was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, was also let out on bail on Thursday. Rowley acknowledged the threat landscape appeared to have changed. “We’re dealing with an increased tempo of terrorists and also of threats that are directed by foreign states such as Iran and Russia,” he said in a radio interview.
